name: Zapoteco de Ayoquezco de Aldama, ZAY

catalog_quote: En ZAY, se puede observar el mismo patrón silábico prosódico que se muestra en la figura 13. [...] Esta regularidad se explica debido a que el ZAY, al igual que otras lenguas zapotecas, posee las siguientes propiedades fonológicas: 1) la lengua posee una condición prosódica con respecto al tamaño mínimo de la palabra fonológica, donde la sílaba acentuada tiene que ser obligatoriamente bimoraica, 2) las consonantes fortis son moraicas, mientras que las lenis no tienen esta propiedad; 3) la vocal se alarga para cumplir el requerimiento de tamaño mínimo de la palabra fonológica, en los casos en los que es necesario. [...] En la figura 19 se observa la representación fonológica de las palabras [ɡɨ2.sɨŋ1] 'ollita' y [ɡɨ:21.sɨŋ1] 'cigarrito'. Se observan que en estos casos ambas palabras poseen dos sílabas, y tres moras que conforman un forman un pie. [...] Además, no se hace una descripción detallada de otros fenómenos relevantes, como, por ejemplo, el acento y su comportamiento fonético o la sílaba y su estructura.

new_statements.translation: In ZAY [Ayoquezco Zapotec] the same syllabic-prosodic pattern shown in figure 13 can be observed. [...] This regularity is explained by the fact that ZAY, like other Zapotec languages, has the following phonological properties: 1) the language has a prosodic condition on the minimal size of the phonological word, whereby the stressed syllable must obligatorily be bimoraic; 2) fortis consonants are moraic while lenis ones are not; 3) the vowel lengthens to meet the minimal-word requirement [...]. (p.144:) Moreover, no detailed description is given of other relevant phenomena, such as, for example, stress and its phonetic behaviour.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Tone language (H, L, rising, falling on nouns; 3 level tones per Cuevas 2023). Words are built on an obligatorily bimoraic stressed syllable: monosyllables (the great majority of monomorphemic words) form a bimoraic foot; the disyllables diagrammed (root + diminutive suffix, e.g. [gɨ2.sɨŋ1] 'ollita', Fig. 19) are parsed as a heavy trochee [[μμ]μ] with the head on the first (root) syllable, following Sicoli's (2007:68) 'binary trochaic foot with a heavy nucleus'. I.e. stress = the root syllable, initial/penultimate in native disyllables. The author explicitly says stress placement and its phonetics were not investigated in detail; the statement is structural (moraic/foot analysis), not a survey of stress position across word types.
new_statements.exceptions: None discussed; disyllabic nouns are said to be mostly compounds, possessed forms or Spanish loans (p.124 n.19), whose stress is not analysed.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word = foot; data are 847 nouns (monosyllabic, disyllabic, diminutives) recorded in isolation (citation forms) from three speakers >60 in Ayoquezco de Aldama; verbs and phrases not examined.
new_statements.identity_note: Both ENAH theses describe the speech of Santa María Ayoquezco de Aldama itself (autonym [ˈdi2.se1]/'díse'), i.e. ayoq1235 proper; Smith Stark's 'Ejutla occidental' grouping (followed by both authors) also covers Santa Cruz Nexila, San Andrés Zabache and San Martín Lachila, which Ethnologue lists under zaf. Lizárraga's stress statement is imported from Sicoli 2007 (Western/Lachixío-area Zapotec) and asserted to hold for Ayoquezco on the basis of his own duration measurements.

sources.note: Tone language (level H/L + rising/falling on nouns). Sec. 1.5, pp.72-73: ZAY has a minimal-word condition in which 'la sílaba acentuada tiene que ser obligatoriamente bimoraica'; fortis codas are moraic; Figs. 17-19 (pp.73-75) parse monosyllables as a bimoraic foot and disyllables (e.g. [gɨ2.sɨŋ1] 'ollita') as a heavy trochee with the bimoraic head on the first syllable, explicitly following Sicoli (2007:68) 'binary trochaic foot with a heavy nucleus'. Autonym transcribed [ˈdi2.se1] (p.5). p.124: most monomorphemic words are monosyllabic. p.144: author states stress and its phonetics were NOT…
